All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data 1 . It was the latest in a run of quarters with nearly $10 billion or more in funding. Funding to the robotics sector in Q1 through Q3 2026 is up around 185% year over year. China and the US lead The bulk of robotics funding this year has been in China, with $13.2 billion invested, and the U.S., with $12.1 billion. Germany, the third-largest recipient of robotics startup funding, trails with $1.7 billion invested. The largest rounds in China went to Guangzhou-based Xpeng Robotics , a builder of AI models and physical robots that raised $900 million, and Shenzhen’s AI² Robotics , which is working to build intelligent robots for manufacturing, healthcare and services and raised a $736 million Series C round. In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick ’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI , which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain. Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics , which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence. Building out the data and model layer “We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen , co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord , a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month. The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said. Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen. We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted. More winners Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three  years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others. Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year. “There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen. payload.text: In an S-1 filing today preceding what could be the largest IPO ever , Anthropic laid out extensive new details about its earnings, growth, key stakeholders and the risks it faces going forward. Clocking in at 335 pages, the document wasn’t exactly light reading. However, after a preliminary once-over, we highlight a few of the more intriguing disclosures below: Revenue growth is unusually rapid For the first half of this year, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.3 billion. That’s up 14x from the same period in 2025. Things aren’t slowing either. While the S-1 doesn’t forecast the second half of this year, Reuters has reported that Anthropic could reach a $110 billion annualized revenue run rate by year-end, citing analysts who met with company executives. But losses persist Anthropic also posted a $693 million operating income loss for the first half of 2026, down about two-thirds from last year. Its net loss for this year’s first half was $80 billion, of which about 90% stemmed from what it called a “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE s.” Founders hold similar stakes Each of Anthropic’s seven founders holds between 230,000 and 246,000 shares of Class A stock, per the S-1. This kind of egalitarianism seems unusual given that startup prospectuses usually show a founding CEO with a much larger relative stake compared to co-founders. The company’s co-founders include Dario Amodei , Daniela Amodei , Tom Brown , Jack Clark , Jared Kaplan , Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah . Anthropic’s risk factors take up 93 pages of its IPO filing So, is investing in Anthropic a risky bet? Anthropic certainly seems to think so. The company’s IPO prospectus contains a staggering 93 pages of risk factors. They start at page 27 and end on page 120. Some are pretty mundane. For instance, the company is concerned that slower revenue growth could potentially constrain its ability to fund frontier AI development and attract and retain top talent. Having incurred significant debt to date, it’s worried about the ability to keep servicing those obligations while still covering operating costs. But more unusual risks, like rogue AI agents, are in there too. In one section, Antrophic notes that “future models are expected to demonstrate capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons.” Related Crunchbase query: Global IPOs For Venture-Backed Companies In 2026 Related reading: Oura Hits Pause On IPO While Anthropic’s Prospectus Reveals The Cost Of Its AI Ambitions The AI IPO Wave Is The Dot-Com Bubble’s Evil Twin. title: When Traction Becomes Personal Exposure: What The Joonko Guilty Plea Means For Founders
summary: By Kyle Jeziorski Ilit Raz , founder and former CEO of the AI startup Joonko , raised roughly $27 million after telling investors the company had customers it never had and revenue it never actually earned. payload.text: By Kyle Jeziorski Ilit Raz , founder and former CEO of the AI startup Joonko , raised roughly $27 million after telling investors the company had customers it never had and revenue it never actually earned. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders. Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud . She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison. Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court. Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research . The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction. Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud Kyle Jeziorski of Founder Shield. The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability. Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred: LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.” Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth. Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue. Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own. Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest? Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims. An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout. Where D&O coverage may stop Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends. As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage. Three policy provisions deserve attention: The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions. Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted. Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances. D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced. Practical steps for founders before presenting metrics Before sharing a pitch deck, create an easily accessible guide for your team that spells out your math. Specify what counts as a paying customer, how pilots and LOIs are classified, and how recurring revenue and churn are calculated. Use those definitions consistently. Team with finance and legal advisers to connect material claims to supporting records, including executed contracts, invoices, accounting data and customer-status reports. Keep projections separate from current results, and document the assumptions behind the forecasts. Don’t confuse ARR with cash collected; they do not belong in the same category. Show clearly how the company calculates recurring revenue and distinguishes it from one-time fees, pipeline opportunities and contracted commitments that haven’t gone live yet. Remember that ARR and contracted ARR are distinct metrics, not to be used interchangeably. Lastly, date the figures and update material changes before investors rely on them for decision-making. If the team can’t explain how they calculate a number or substantiate a customer claim, resolve the discrepancy before presenting your deck. Investors might buy into your vision, but regulators will look at your math. Kyle Jeziorski is the market-facing and client leader at Founder Shield, the innovation arm of The Baldwin Group , with eight years invested in the boutique broker and more than a decade in the insurance industry. Before Founder Shield, he worked at Marsh on the FINPRO team focusing on management liability in the large private and public space. A graduate of Saint Joseph’s University ’s risk management and insurance program, Jeziorski has focused his entire career helping clients navigate through an ever-changing risk environment. As investment hit unprecedented levels in 2026, Golden State companies alone raised more than all U.S. startups in any prior year on record. Yet California companies have already pulled in an unparalleled $385 billion in seed- through growth-stage rounds. That’s more than double last year’s tally. California’s share of U.S. startup funding also has been trending higher for the past three years. Much of this is due to San Francisco AI unicorns, but we’re also seeing strength in the broader Silicon Valley region as well as Southern California. Where the money went Flabbergasting financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic account for more than half of this year’s California statewide tally. But even without those, California companies 1 still secured a disproportionate share of the largest U.S. equity funding rounds. To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 next-largest California funding rounds this year. Some of these are familiar names and involve fairly mature companies. For instance Waymo , which launched inside Google in 2009 and spun out as an independent company 10 years ago, picked up $16 billion in February. Another old-timer is Databricks , which picked up $5 billion in August. It’s now 13 years old and has raised over $30 billion in debt and equity funding to date. Still, we’re also seeing younger companies secure megarounds. Prometheus , the physical AI startup co-founded and led by Jeff Bezos and launched last year, pulled in $12 billion in new funding this spring. And AI model startup Safe Superintelligence landed $5 billion in a Nvidia -led round this summer. Early-stage funding That brings us to our next point. California’s startup funding windfall isn’t only about late-stage and pre-IPO companies bagging enormous rounds. Early- and seed-stage companies are also attracting big checks from investors. Per Crunchbase data, California companies have secured nearly $62 billion in seed- and early-stage financings so far in 2026. That’s roughly 57% of all U.S. funding at these stages. It’s also far above prior year tallies, as charted below, and appears to be a record funding level. Don’t bet against California If there’s a lesson to be learned in these numbers, it’s one that savvy startup investors ought to have learned a long time ago: Don’t bet against California. Whatever the year, whatever the technology cycle, California, and Silicon Valley in particular, have a knack for being home to the leading companies of the era. payload.text: By Seth Kugler If you only have six months of experience in an industry, you usually aren’t equipped to poach your employer’s clients and start a competing business. Of course, you may believe otherwise if you plan to use your employer’s proprietary information to train an AI agent to do the heavy lifting for you. Seth Kugler, partner at Grellas Shah LLP. That is exactly what the defendant attempted in a recent federal trade secrets case I litigated on behalf of a client in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. In that case, the defendant, a former senior employee at the marketing agency, didn’t just copy client lists to solicit accounts. Instead, he used stolen trade secrets as training inputs to build, essentially, an AI version of his old boss , attempting a shortcut to create a competing business without spending years developing the skills and expertise typically needed to provide such services. AI is creating new ways to misappropriate trade secrets, well beyond the classic theft story of an employee downloading files onto a thumb drive. This case highlights a new reality for founders, exposing unprecedented risks related to AI and trade secrets, employee use of personal devices, and the heightened need for companies to protect themselves in the age of agentic AI. Key lessons for founders AI contamination cannot be undone The defense in this case argued that because their client placed the stolen documents in a “quarantine folder” and no clients had been poached yet, no harm had been done. The court appropriately recognized that the “quarantine folder” was grossly insufficient, granting our temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction while recognizing the competing AI agent as an “existential threat.” An agreement not to touch just the stolen documents themselves is essentially irrelevant once AI gets involved: If a trade secret is used to develop a machine learning model or used to train an AI agent with recursive capabilities, it contaminates the model and the impact can be difficult to undo. Even if raw source files are completely scrubbed of any direct evidence of stolen materials, defendants will struggle to prove to courts that the AI isn’t operating a certain way precisely because it once had access to that proprietary information. Personal devices can pose big risks While trade secret misappropriation has typically been malicious, AI now also creates significant risks of inadvertent violations. Startups frequently scale with employees working on personal devices under standard Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreements. Running desktop AI agents on these devices can pose a serious risk. Unlike standard web interfaces, a desktop AI agent can scan files, create folders and ingest directory paths across a local hard drive, often without requiring special permission or alerting the user. Right now, thousands of employees may be inadvertently violating confidentiality agreements by running consumer AI agents on personal laptops that house their employers’ IP. If settings allow model training from this data, courts may eventually find these trade secrets to have lost legal protection due to dissemination outside the company. Standard IT audits won’t catch AI data theft This recent case serves as a warning for how attorneys and founders must approach trade secret investigations. Traditional digital discovery is no longer sufficient because AI tools make it effortless to disperse, alter and recreate data across nonobvious folder paths. Actions that previously seemed like overkill — such as full forensic imaging of a personal device — are now the bare minimum. Furthermore, AI dramatically reduces the friction of reverse-engineering software and tech products, potentially removing telltale signs that code or data was copied. Proving theft in AI contexts requires intensive, highly technical expert analysis and carries far more uncertainty than traditional IP litigation. 3 practical steps companies should take Founders should take three legal and operational steps to proactively protect their business: Implement strict agentic AI policies: Mandate tight controls and settings that isolate outside AI from company documents. Web-based tools like Claude with strict data privacy policies are vastly safer than open source or desktop apps that crawl local drives. Some AI agents should not be permitted to run at all within an environment containing trade secrets. Eliminate remote access from unmanaged devices: Shift to a closed cloud environment where data can be viewed and manipulated on a secure server, but files cannot be downloaded locally to a personal desktop. Removing local file downloads eliminates the risk of desktop AI agents indexing proprietary data. Rewrite your Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreements for the AI era: Standard confidentiality agreements need explicit clauses addressing AI use, model training inputs, and a precise definition of data misappropriation through machine learning. If you suspect an employee has walked away with data or misused it in an AI tool, your first step should be immediate: cut off all system access and retain counsel. Don’t wait until you start losing clients or experiencing financial losses. Feeding trade secrets into AI presents an existential threat from day one. AI gives individuals the unprecedented ability to compete in spaces where they lack experience, making proprietary data more vulnerable than ever. Modernizing security, policy and legal strategies to address today’s AI threats will help startups and established companies avoid catastrophic exposure. Seth Kugler is a partner at Grellas Shah LLP , where he focuses on complex commercial litigation, including disputes related to trade secret and IP misappropriation, corporate governance and breach of fiduciary duties, breach of contract, and other complex business disputes. He specializes in preventing and resolving all manner of disputes among and between corporate founders, directors, officers and shareholders, LLC members, and other current and former business partners. payload.text: This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here . From teaching robots to do everyday household chores to using lasers to track satellites in space, this month’s crop of interesting startup deals spans some decidedly different corners of tech. Other startups that caught our eye are working on making cement production less polluting, turning agricultural waste into a useful tool for carbon removal, and helping independent video game developers get their product in front of more players. Let’s take a closer look. $30M to teach robots by watching humans Before robots can fold laundry, load dishwashers or prepare meals, they need to learn how humans actually do those things. Maxinsights is betting there’s a big business in supplying the training material. The Santa Clara, California-based startup this week announced a $30 million seed round led by Peak XV Partners , with participation from Tola Capital , South Park Commons , Ince Capital and Alumni Ventures . The company, founded by veterans of the robotics and autonomous vehicle industries, is building what it calls the data layer for physical AI. Its approach is surprisingly low-tech in some respects: Pay people to wear cameras while they go about everyday tasks, from washing dishes to preparing food or cleaning hotel rooms. But turning all that footage into something useful for robotics models is more complicated. Maxinsights develops its own recording hardware and AI-powered software to collect, label and organize the data so robots can learn from it. The startup says it has already captured more than 2 million hours of human activity, with 1.5 million hours ready for use in AI training. Its customers include robotics model developers Genesis AI and Dyna Robotics . It is also developing a sensor-equipped glove called MaxGlove that can capture information cameras can’t see, such as grip strength and the force needed to manipulate objects. The funding comes amid a massive boom in physical AI investment. Startups in the sector raised $47.4 billion globally in the first half of 2026 , nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, Crunchbase data shows. Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026 £8.2M to track satellites with lasers Space is getting crowded, and keeping track of everything flying around up there is becoming an increasingly complicated problem. With that in mind, London-based Foundational emerged from stealth this month with £8.2 million (around $11 million) in pre-seed funding led by Inflection , with participation from investors including Type One Ventures , Final Frontier, Backed VC and Adjacent . The company uses a technique called satellite laser ranging, which involves firing laser pulses from ground stations toward reflectors mounted on satellites. The company says that by measuring how long the light takes to return, its system can calculate satellite positions with millimeter-level accuracy. While the technology has existed for decades, Foundational is working to make it cheaper and more scalable. Its system combines automated ground stations, satellite-mounted hardware and a software platform called Origin that provides positioning data to satellite operators. The company says its stations cost roughly 30x less than legacy systems. The technology could prove increasingly valuable as thousands more satellites enter orbit, raising the risk of collisions with other spacecraft and debris. The European Space Agency estimates that around 1.5 million pieces of space debris measuring between 1 and 10 centimeters are orbiting Earth — large enough to cause serious damage to functioning satellites. Foundational’s raise comes amid a record-setting year for space technology funding. Investors had already poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally by late August , Crunchbase data shows, easily surpassing previous annual records with several months still left in the year. Related Crunchbase query: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding $10M to make cement without so much carbon Cement is the glue holding much of the modern world together. It’s also responsible for roughly 8% of global carbon dioxide emissions , per an MIT estimate. Calgary, Canada-based Cura Climate wants to change that. The startup last month said it raised $10 million in new funding led by Zacua Ventures , with participation from Sandpiper Ventures , Amplify Capital and Vantage Futures , to advance technology that could substantially reduce emissions from cement production. Cement manufacturing traditionally requires heating limestone to extremely high temperatures, a process that releases significant amounts of carbon dioxide. Cura is developing an electrochemical alternative that uses electricity to separate carbon dioxide from limestone before it enters the kiln. The company says its process could cut cement-related emissions by up to 85% while also reducing energy consumption. Crucially, the technology is designed to integrate with existing cement plants rather than requiring manufacturers to replace their entire production facilities. The fresh capital will help fund a pilot plant in Alberta capable of producing 100 metric tons of material annually, as well as engineering work for a larger commercial demonstration facility with a planned capacity of 30,000 metric tons per year. Cura is among a growing crop of startups targeting industrial processes that have proven particularly difficult to decarbonize. While venture funding for cleantech has fallen well below the peaks of 2021 and 2022, the sector has shown signs of stabilizing. Investors put $15 billion into cleantech-, EV- and sustainability-related startups in the first half of 2026 , with second-quarter investment reaching its highest level since 2024, Crunchbase data shows. Startups like Cura working on cleaner cement technologies , in particular, have also seen investor interest in recent years. Related Crunchbase query: Global Cleantech Startup Funding In 2026 $10M to help mobile games find their players Making a successful mobile game is one thing. Getting enough people to discover and play it is an entirely different — and often very expensive — challenge. Cyprus-based Mika Games is tackling that problem with an unusual investment model. The company, founded by Wargaming co-founder Nick Katselapov , said this week that it had raised $10 million in new funding led by Flint Capital to help early-stage gaming studios turn promising titles into commercial successes. Mika isn’t a traditional game developer. Instead, it invests in small studios and helps finance the expensive marketing campaigns needed to attract players. The problem is something of a catch-22 for developers: They often need hundreds of thousands of dollars in advertising to prove that their games can attract and retain paying users. But the financing providers that fund those campaigns typically want several months of marketing performance data before they’ll provide capital. Mika aims to bridge that gap by combining equity investments in game development with separate financing for early marketing campaigns. If those efforts demonstrate that a game can acquire players profitably, the studio may then qualify for larger financing arrangements. The company says it now has five studios in its portfolio, including the developer of Legendale, a farming adventure game with more than 3 million players, and Punko, a tower defense game with more than 500,000 downloads. The investment comes as gaming startup funding is showing signs of recovery. Companies in the sector had raised around $2 billion globally in 2026 as of late September , already exceeding the full-year 2025 total, Crunchbase data shows. Mika isn’t the only investor experimenting with alternative financing for game developers. Griffin Gaming Partners earlier this year announced a $100 million fund offering indie studios financing in exchange for a share of game revenue, another sign that investors see opportunities beyond conventional equity funding in the gaming industry. Related Crunchbase query: Gaming-Related Startup Funding, 2026 $3M to turn coffee waste into carbon removal Not that you need another reason to look forward to your steaming morning cup of coffee, but consider this: The leftovers from that daily ritual might eventually help remove carbon from the atmosphere. Zurich-based Cotierra said late last month that it had raised $3 million in funding co-led by PINC, the venture arm of food and beverage company Paulig , and Carbon Removal Partners . Cotierra says it’s developing technology that turns agricultural waste into biochar, a charcoal-like material that can store carbon for long periods while improving soil health. Biochar itself isn’t new. What’s interesting about Cotierra’s approach is where and how it wants to make it. Rather than transporting bulky crop residues to large centralized facilities, the startup says it’s developing smaller, decentralized reactors that can be deployed close to where agricultural waste is generated. Its technology combines the reactors with software to monitor production, track the resulting carbon removal, and verify the environmental benefits. The company has initially focused on Colombia’s coffee-growing regions, including Huila, the Coffee Triangle, Antioquia and Santander, where growers face increasing pressure to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. Cotierra says its technology has already been tested on coffee farms and is now moving toward larger commercial deployments, with plans to expand into cocoa, cotton and citrus production. It’s a potentially appealing business model for both farmers and food companies: Turn an otherwise low-value waste product into something that can improve soil conditions while also generating measurable carbon removal. Its raise, however, comes against a difficult backdrop for agricultural technology investment. Global funding to agriculture and farming startups remains far below its 2021 peak, when companies in the sector raised $10.5 billion, according to a Crunchbase News analysis earlier this year . Funding to the sector totaled just $2.8 billion through the third quarter of 2026, down even from the $3.5 billion raised in the same period last year. payload.text: Slingshot Insurance , an AI-native embedded insurance startup, is emerging from stealth with $27 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Rally Ventures and Skyward Group co-led the round, with participation from insurance industry veterans including Jim Hays , who will join Slingshot’s board. Rally is also a co-founder of the Minneapolis-based startup, as part of the firm’s broader approach. So far, it has co-founded roughly eight portfolio companies that have either launched or remain in stealth. Ethan Genteman, co-founder and CEO of Slingshot Insurance. (Courtesy photo) Slingshot, which is led by first-time founder and CEO Ethan Genteman , focuses on small insurance policies that consumers can buy as part of another purchase, such as coverage when booking a flight. Known as embedded insurance, the model puts coverage in front of customers when they might need it. The startup’s software helps businesses offer those policies by connecting them with insurers that back the coverage. It uses AI to process and share data between the two sides, aiming to reduce the administrative work that can make inexpensive policies costly to offer. Its first customer and design partner is Vertical Insure , which serves more than 750,000 customers at an average premium of $25, according to Slingshot. Genteman told Crunchbase News that Slingshot’s first program will launch this month. For now, Slingshot earns revenue as a technology provider working with outside insurers. But the six-person company, which formally began operating July 1, is also pursuing an acquisition that would allow it to back policies itself. “We’re not a carrier yet, but we are rapidly closing on our carrier,” Genteman said in an interview. Making the math work on a $25 policy One product Slingshot is working on would let parents buy insurance when signing a child up for youth sports, Genteman said. A parent spending $2,000 on a volleyball league, for example, might be offered a $25 policy covering cancellation or an injury during the season. Each policy includes paperwork and coordination with an insurer, and can bring potential claims. But when policies cost so little, managing them can quickly eat into the money they bring in, noted Genteman. He believes that as vertical SaaS companies increasingly look beyond traditional subscription fees for growth, embedded insurance is “a largely untapped opportunity” to generate incremental revenue from transactions already happening on their platforms while delivering additional value to customers. “The challenge is that the insurance and regulatory landscape is incredibly complex, and most SaaS companies don’t have the expertise, industry relationships or understanding of where to begin,” he said. Slingshot aims to solve this by providing a white-glove service for those vertical SaaS companies, helping them go from an insurance product idea to “a fully operational offering.” He offered a hypothetical example: A program collecting $500,000 in premiums with a 10% margin would have just $50,000 in margin. “That’s not a viable program for the way incumbent carriers have set themselves up operationally,” he said. Slingshot’s goal is to replace the spreadsheets, emails and disconnected systems used to manage that work with software that connects policy distributors and insurers directly. The company says its AI automates data-heavy tasks while keeping a record of decisions that the businesses involved can review and check. It charges a 5% technology fee to administer programs through its platform. Acquiring an insurer would let it provide both the software and the financial backing, according to Genteman. A customer helped shape the business The difficulties facing Slingshot’s first customer helped bring the startup together. Rally had already helped start Vertical Insure, which uses software platforms to sell insurance to its customers. According to Genteman, that business had opportunities to introduce more products but struggled to find insurers whose technology and processes could keep up. “We can design the products our customers need almost overnight, but the industry is highly regulated, and we need delegated authority just to write and distribute what we’ve built,” Vertical Insure co-founder and CEO Brock Noland said in a statement. “The antiquated approval process on the carrier-side slows everything down.” Even after finding an insurer willing to back a product, connecting the two companies’ systems could create more delays, Genteman said. Slingshot was built to address those problems, with Vertical Insure helping shape its product as a design partner. Noland is also a Slingshot co-founder. The opportunity in vertical SaaS Genteman sees a broader opening among vertical SaaS companies: businesses that sell software tailored to a particular industry. As vertical SaaS companies look for ways to grow beyond subscription fees, insurance could give them another avenue to make money from purchases customers already make through their platforms, argues Genteman. They already know their customers and what they’re buying, putting them in a position to offer coverage that fits the purchase. A babysitting platform, for example, could offer coverage to help parents pay for replacement childcare if a sitter cancels at the last minute. Software used by pet boarding facilities could offer coverage for unexpected vet bills if a pet is injured during a stay. An equipment rental platform could let customers add protection at checkout against accidental damage or theft. Those are examples of what could be developed, Genteman said. Slingshot aims to help vertical SaaS companies take ideas like those and turn them into insurance they can sell, providing both the software and help navigating the insurance industry and its regulatory requirements. “Insurance becomes another product that can be offered naturally within the existing customer experience,” he said. For Justin Kaufenberg , managing director at Rally Ventures, that opportunity is familiar. Before joining Rally, he ran SportsEngine , where insurance sold through its software became a key revenue source. “That experience gave me firsthand insight into the opportunity for software companies to generate revenue through embedded financial products,” he wrote via email. Kaufenberg sees similar potential across Rally’s portfolio, where most companies combine AI products with financial services. He said founders increasingly want insurance partners that can help them introduce coverage quickly. Rally co-founded Slingshot to bring insurance backing, underwriting, reporting, claims handling and distribution together in one business. “To get the carrier, the reinsurance, the underwriting platform, the data flow engine, the reporting capabilities, the claims handling, the embedded distribution engine, and every other part of the offering from a single vendor is unheard of,” Kaufenberg said. From insurance executive to founder Before starting Slingshot, Genteman was chief actuarial officer at publicly traded Palomar Holdings , where he also led data. He joined in 2019 and helped build its actuarial and data team as the company expanded beyond earthquake insurance into other coverage types. That work led him to explore whether newer technology could reduce the costs of running insurance programs. About a year ago, he began coding and building prototypes in his basement. He started talking with Rally toward the end of 2025 and left Palomar on July 1 to run Slingshot. Related Crunchbase query: Insurtech Startup Funding, 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: By Anurag Gurtu When a company delays its IPO to show investors better numbers, that’s a strategy. When the NYC pension fund publicly asks you to delay it over AI safety concerns, your chief rival’s CEO calls his own IPO “ill-advised” and postpones it until at least next year, tech stocks are sliding on open-weight model fears, and your own prospectus warns of “existential risks to humanity” from the product you’re selling, that’s not a strategy. That’s a market sending you a message. Anthropic ‘s numbers are extraordinary. Its third-quarter 2026 revenue was reportedly $16.8 billion — up 45% quarter on quarter. That means the company’s annualized revenue run rate is roughly $67 billion. What the S-1 actually says Anurag Gurtu, co-founder and CEO of Airrived. Here are the numbers from Anthropic’s leaked prospectus : $4.6 billion: Anthropic’s full-year 2025 revenue. $7.33 billion : What Anthropic spent on compute and infrastructure in 2025 alone — more than its total revenue. $42 billion: Anthropic’s net loss in 2025. The roadshow will immediately explain that $34 billion of it was a noncash accounting charge — an adjustment to the estimated value of financing instruments that could eventually convert into shares. $518 billion: How much Anthropic expects to spend, at least, over the course of a decade on AI infrastructure with six partners, including Google , Microsoft and Amazon , according to the confidential IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters . About 80% of the total is noncancelable or payable regardless of usage. $2 trillion: That’s the IPO valuation Anthropic is still targeting for November, a figure representing 435x its 2025 revenue. One more number from the S-1 that the roadshow will bury: A quarter of Anthropic’s 2025 revenue came from two unnamed customers. Three signals the market is sending The IPO delay is the headline. It isn’t the only signal worth reading. Signal one: NYC Comptroller Mark Levine. Last week, the supervisor of New York City’s pension funds — which reportedly hold roughly $7 million in Anthropic exposure today, but could hold dramatically more if Anthropic enters the Russell 3000 post-IPO — sent a letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urging the company to pause the IPO entirely. The risks he cited are the same ones Anthropic’s own prospectus flags: increasingly autonomous AI systems that could behave in unexpected ways, create security problems, and in the document’s own language, pose “existential risks to humanity.” Signal two: Sam Altman delays OpenAI ’s IPO. OpenAI has said it will not go public in 2026. CEO Altman called an IPO at this moment “ill-advised” given AI safety concerns, and while that framing is partly strategic — positioning OpenAI as the more responsible actor — it’s also a real signal when the CEO of the second-most valuable AI company in the world looks at current conditions and decides to wait. Signal three: The chip selloff. Last week’s $2 trillion chip-stock selloff was driven partly by concern over AI-buildout costs. Gartner ’s forecast helps explain the concern: Through 2030, it sees at most $3.6 trillion in revenue attributable to AI data centers, versus $8.5 trillion needed to cover planned investment, financing costs and a 12% return. The open-weight problem Here is the structural argument that no amount of Q3 revenue growth resolves: Anthropic’s $2 trillion valuation requires closed-model AI to maintain a durable pricing premium over open-weight alternatives. That premium is being systematically dismantled. Open-weight AI is challenging the economics behind closed-model valuations. Enterprise adoption rose from 23% to 67% in 2026, with companies reporting 70%–90% cost savings. DeepSeek R1 offers frontier-level performance on most enterprise benchmarks at 7 cents per million input tokens; independent analysis puts Anthropic’s comparable input and output pricing at roughly 18x and 23x higher, respectively. DeepSeek’s weights are free to download, allowing enterprises to self-host without a model-provider API contract or per-token billing, while the capability gap with closed models reportedly closes within six months of a frontier release. Against that backdrop, New Constructs — the research firm that called Anthropic’s proposed offering “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility” — calculated that justifying a $2 trillion valuation would require an immediate 10% after-tax operating margin sustained for a decade, extraordinary revenue growth, and $358 billion in annual after-tax operating profit by 2035. Why this is worse than 1999 The dot-com bubble had a genuine excuse. Nobody knew what the internet would become. The AI IPO wave of 2026 does not have that excuse. Worldwide spending on AI is forecast to reach $2.59 trillion in 2026 , up 47% year over year, according to Gartner. Yet a July 2025 MIT NANDA report estimated that 95% of the organizations it examined were getting no return from generative AI. Meanwhile, KPMG said in its own report earlier this year that just 7% of surveyed leaders say they’ve established ROI from AI. This is the context in which Anthropic is asking investors to pay 435x 2025 revenue for a company with $518 billion in locked infrastructure commitments, 25% revenue concentration in two unnamed clients, and a pricing moat that open-weight models are closing in six-month cycles. The delay from October to November doesn’t change any of those numbers. It adds one quarter of revenue data. What actually survives this correction Here is what no AI IPO roadshow will say out loud: The biggest enterprise AI winners will not necessarily own the most expensive model. They will own the architecture that turns any model into governed, auditable, measurable outcomes — through proprietary enterprise data, domain-specific fine-tuning, multiagent orchestration and controls that make autonomous execution trustworthy. That value does not depend on keeping model capabilities scarce or securing a $2 trillion valuation. It compounds in production, where customers understand that the model is not the product. The deployment is. The dot-com crash did not happen because the internet was bad. It happened because the price was wrong. AI investors face the same distinction: Real technology does not automatically justify its valuation. A strong quarter and a one-month delay do not close that gap. November simply gives Anthropic more time to explain the math. Anurag Gurtu , the co-founder and CEO of Airrived , is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk , Tripwire and Sun Microsystems , and a public company, FireEye . He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification. title: storerouter
summary: Shop via CLI; for agents and software engineers

extra.author: marram
extra.original_title: Show HN: Shop via CLI; for agents and software engineers

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

We're building a single search/browse API interface to thousands of ecommerce stores (hopefully, eventually, all of them). Inspired by Shopify's https://shop.dev, we embedded a WASM bridge of our CLI in our website.

The idea is to provide an efficient commerce interface for agents; personal assistants (Instinct et al) or otherwise. The alternatives are to build a crawling system / Firecrawl, use an LLM search api (Exa, Parallel etc) or use embedded headless browsers. Collective action by brands/retailers to implement agentic-protocols (UCP, ACP etc) is unlikely; so we're doing it for them.

Surprisingly, despite our coverage list being smaller than Shopify's and the search endpoint being slower (~3k ms for p90; because there is JEV and/or LLM to convert free form search to facets) the search results are often subjectively better:

``` storerouter search 'gold frame pink tint sunglasses' --facet category_path.depth_3=sunglasses --facet temple_color=gold --facet lens_color=pink --facet eyewear_frame_material=metal ```

vs Shop.dev's: ``` shop search 'gold frame pink tint sunglasses' --category gid://shopify/TaxonomyCategory/aa-2-27 # dropped facet temple_color=temple_color__gold (no Shopify filter) # dropped facet lens_color=lens_color__pink (no Shopify filter) # dropped facet eyewear_frame_material=eyewear_frame_material__metal (no Shopify filter) # category 'sunglasses' → Apparel & Accessories > Clothing Accessories > Sunglasses ```

title: Cryo
summary: A language whose programs live forever

extra.author: zwad3
extra.original_title: Show HN: Cryo – A language whose programs live forever

story_text.value:
Cryo is a programming language that models long-running tasks like workflows or AI agents. Programs freeze to disk when idle and can be thawed when new data arrives.

As part of our announcement of Endothermic Labs, we've put together a small demo of Cryo that highlights its features and walks through the language and its plugin system.

We originally built it as a way to deploy healthcare agents at scale, but have rebuilt it from the ground up to be a standalone toolchain for long-running tasks. It acts as something like a cross between Durable Objects and Temporal workflows, where the script itself is the durable unit with no replay needed.

Cryo is statically and structurally typed, with a concurrency model similar to Go. It's still under active development, so we're holding off on open sourcing it until we're confident that the language is stable, ideally in the next 3-4 weeks.

title: withnative
summary: Markdown is 40× more token-efficient with SQLite

extra.author: richardcrng
extra.original_title: Show HN: Markdown is 40× more token-efficient with SQLite

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Richard, founder of Native. I'm working on open-source context ownership, to stop AI centralisation: https://github.com/withnative/native

My first focus has been making Markdown vaults powerful enough so that teams can self-host all of their context (messaging, docs and projects), without it being externally fragmented or rate-limited.

I'm sharing some early results: Markdown vaults can be 40× more efficient with SQLite!

https://www.withnative.ai/research-and-posts/markdown-contex...

Here's some of the main ideas:

- SQLite or Markdown folders, you pick. You can project the same authoritative event log into either form; more projection formats will follow (e.g. maybe neo4j; we do use a graph structure).

- Empirically: SQLite is better for agents! On a 120 trial evaluation for 11,000 records, agents use 40× fewer tokens with SQLite vs Markdown, per correct answer.

- Everything is a file or SQLite row. Messages, documents and projects: all can be modelled in your vault. You get local-first collaboration with teammates, synced to a cloud of your choice.

- You can render your vault with arbitrary UI. Your WhatsApp-like UI speaks to your teammate's Slack-like UI; both are just views over the same database.

A few things I've learned building this:

- Agents do pretty well even without SQL if you give them strongly typed Markdown frontmatter. This was one arm of the trial I ran. I didn't have any clear expectations, but it was cool to watch: agents ended up writing Python scripts to do SQL-like queries.

- Cumulatively, cached input tokens can get expensive. I feel silly in hindsight here. I'd gotten used to letting my sessions run long, "It's all cached so it's very cheap". But when I looked at my results here, over 2/3 of the token bill on long sessions was cached input...

- "Markdown vaults don't scale as well as databases" isn't as self-evident as I think. This is why I decided to benchmark it... I've had some very blank stares when I try to explain how Markdown files might break at true agent-scale volume.

Unfortunately, the dataset is private, because it's two months of my own work. I am considering open-sourcing it even so, but there is definitely some embarrassing stuff in there. TBD... I know that independent result verification matters!

The core engine that I evaluated is open-source, with more to be released soon: https://github.com/withnative/native

If you're interested in trying connected context on an open engine, you can get updates from our website or email me directly: richard@withnative.ai

https://www.withnative.ai/

title: Termcraft
summary: 2D terminal survival with multiplayer support

extra.author: sebosch
extra.original_title: Show HN: Termcraft – 2D terminal survival with multiplayer support

story_text.value:
Earlier this year, I started developing Termcraft, a terminal-based 2D survival game written in Rust.

Since its first release more than half a year ago, I've added multiplayer support, so you can now host a game and play with friends (or colleagues during a meeting?); Up to 8 players. I've also substantially improved the visuals, lighting, physics, and overall gameplay. A friend and I ended up spending the entire weekend playing through the game from start to finish.

The progression takes you from gathering wood and building a shelter to crafting equipment, exploring caves, finding diamonds, crossing the Nether, and fighting the Ender Dragon. There are villages, farming, collaborative building, PvP, and player chat along the way.

It's open source under the AGPL-3.0 license, with downloadable builds for Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Gameplay demo video: https://youtu.be/nn37_15dLFM Installation and controls: https://pagel-s.github.io/termcraft/

It's not perfect, but I'd love to hear your feedback and experiences with the game. Contributions are also more than welcome!

extra.author: pancomplex

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

title: huggingface/transformers: Release: v5.21.0
summary: # Release v5.21.0 ## New Model additions ### MiniCPM-OCR MiniCPM-OCR is a document-understanding model from OpenBMB's MiniCPM-V family. It keeps the MiniCPM-V 4.6 architecture, which pairs a SigLIP vision encoder and a window-attention merger with a Qwen3.5 language model. It is specialized for reading text-dense images such as scanned pages, screenshots, receipts and tables. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/minicpm_ocr) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.18154) * Feat test (#49920) by @guarin in [#49920](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49920) ### Flint Flint is Recursive's mixture-of-experts language model. Compared to a standard SwiGLU MoE transformer such as Qwen3-MoE, it uses hybrid attention (sliding-window attention with rotary embeddings over the current token and the previous 512 tokens in most layers, and full attention without positional encoding in the remaining layers). It also has learned attention sinks, as in GPT-OSS, with per-head RMS-normalized queries and keys. Each sparse layer routes a token to 6 of 256 experts by sigmoid score and adds an ungated shared expert, and the first two layers are dense. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/flint) * Add Flint model support. (#49824) by @lovishmadaan in [#49824](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49824) ### UltraVBert UltraVBert extends ModernVBert by pairing the UltraBERT text encoder with a SigLIP vision encoder for visual document understanding and retrieval. Its image processor splits each page into 512-pixel tiles plus a global view. The connector merges each 4 x 4 block of vision patches into one token, so a tile becomes 64 image tokens, and RMS-normalizes them to the scale of UltraBERT's token embeddings. The `max_image_tiles` setting (27 by default) caps the number of tiles per page. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/ultravbert) * Add UltraVBERT (#49685) by @athrael-soju in [#49685](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49685) ### Gradium Phonon TTS Gradium Phonon TTS is Gradium's family of on-device text-to-speech models, trained with the Pocket TTS recipe. A causal transformer reads a voice prompt and the text, then emits one continuous 32-dimensional audio latent per step at 12.5 Hz through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when the utterance ends. The latents are decoded to 24 kHz audio by a Pocket TTS audio tokenizer. Unlike Pocket TTS, voice conditioning uses 512-dimensional latents from a separate, unreleased speaker codec, so voices come as precomputed latents and cannot be cloned from a recording. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/gradium_phonon_tts) * Add GradiumPhononTTS (#49791) by @eustlb in [#49791](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49791) ### Pocket TTS Pocket TTS is Kyutai's 100M-parameter text-to-speech model, built as a Continuous Audio Language Model that runs faster than real time on CPU. A causal transformer emits one continuous audio latent per frame (12.5 Hz) through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when to stop. A Mimi-based audio tokenizer encodes voice prompts and decodes the generated latents to 24 kHz audio. Two flow heads are released, Lagrangian self-distillation (default) and drifting, and voices can be cloned from a recording, passed as precomputed latents, or loaded from cached KV states. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (the Continuous Audio Language Models paper, arXiv 2509.06926). It is the only paper the documentation links, and it describes the architecture family Pocket TTS belongs to. The docs do not cite a separate Pocket TTS technical report.) | [Blog Post](NONE. The documentation links no official blog post. It points only to the original code repository at https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts.) * add PocketTTS (#49589) by @eustlb in [#49589](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49589) ### Pocket TTS Audio Tokenizer The Pocket TTS audio tokenizer is the codec used by Pocket TTS. It has Mimi's architecture (SEANet convolutions plus a small causal transformer on each side), but its residual vector quantizer is replaced by a continuous 32-dimensional bottleneck, the VAE-GAN from Continuous Audio Language Models. It converts 24 kHz audio into latents at 12.5 Hz and decodes them back to audio. It serves as the `audio_tokenizer` of `PocketTTSProcessor`, encoding voice prompts and decoding generated latents, and its encoder and decoder can also be loaded on their own. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts_audio_tokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (Continuous Audio Language Models, whose VAE-GAN this tokenizer uses; arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06926)) * add PocketTTSAudioTokenizer (#49588) by @eustlb in [#49588](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49588) ## Breaking changes Fixed Gemma4 processor imports (the Gemma4, Gemma4 unified and EmbeddingGemma2 processors) so `from transformers import *` no longer fails in environments that have `PIL` but not `torch`; no user action is needed. * :rotating_light: Fix gemma4 cross imports resulting in import failing without `torch` but with `PIL` (#49748) by @Sai-Suraj-27 Added an `"fp8"` backend to `QuantizedCache`, alongside `quanto` and `hqq`, that stores KV states in `torch.float8_e4m3fn` with a single scale per tensor; enable it with `cache_implementation="quantized"` and `cache_config={"backend": "fp8"}`. * 🚨Add an FP8 backend to `QuantizedCache` (#48677) by @jiqing-feng Tensor parallelism now has a dedicated embedding style, shards every model's input embeddings by default, and supports widths that aren't divisible by the TP size, so `ColwiseParallel` and `RowwiseParallel` now apply only to linear layers; custom TP plans that applied them to embeddings must switch to the new embedding style. * 🚨 TP: give embeddings their own style, shard input embeddings by default, and shard widths that don't divide by the TP size (#49570) by @IlyasMoutawwakil Every MoE TP and EP plan now shards its experts, so models no longer keep all experts on every rank, and a new `test_moe_parallel_plans_shard_experts` test enforces this; custom or downstream MoE parallel plans must add expert sharding to pass it and to avoid wasted memory. * 🚨 MoE: shard the experts in every TP/EP plan, and test for it (#49206) by @IlyasMoutawwakil ## Cache This release improves cache handling across the library. Flash Attention now works with static caches, BLOOM no longer crashes with static cache or compiled generate, chunked prefill supports cache continuation, and the Qwen4-Exp indexer's position history stays aligned with its cached keys. Linear-attention caches also gain new getters (`is_recording_past`, `get_recurrent_state`, conv-state access) that stop exposing cache internals and prepare for paged-c * [FA] Fix FA with static cache (#49998) by @Cyrilvallez in [#49998] * [docs] CB cache behavior (#49025) by @stevhliu in [#49025] * [CB] Reduce warmup time by not computing attention over full cache (#49853) by @remi-or in [#49853] * Fix Qwen4-Exp indexer position cache lifecycle (#49840) by @taking-lying-flat in [#49840] * [Cache] Linear attn cache: use new getters (#49375) by @remi-or in [#49375] * [Cache] Get conv states (#49309) by @remi-or in [#49309] * [Cache] Add get_recurrent_state (#49306) by @remi-or in [#49306] * [Cache] Add is_recording_past (#49305) by @remi-or in [#49305] * Fix BLOOM crash with static cache / compiled generate (#49481) by @kaixuanliu in [#49481] * Allow Cache continuation for chunked prefill (#49662) by @Cyrilvallez in [#49662] ## Vision Vision image processors now composite PNG transparency onto white instead of exposing black pixels, and `background_color` is preserved correctly across the DeepSeek-VL and Janus processors. Model fixes cover SmolVLM's `inputs_merger` when image tokens aren't a multiple of the patch size, HunYuan-VL image assignment during batched beam search, and Ernie4.5-VL-MoE expert sharding under TP/EP. The DETR * Composite transparency in shared RGB conversion and image processors (#49079) by @Nikhi00718 in [#49079] * [Fetcher] Fix missing test deps for dynamically-resolved image processors (#49826) by @ydshieh in [#49826] * fix(vision): Route the DETR conversion scripts through from_pretrained (#49830) by @harshaljanjani in [#49830] * Fix background_color handling across DeepSeek-VL and Janus image processors (#49767) by @tritsystem in [#49767] * Move the MI300 docker image to ROCm 10.1 and update test expectations (#49460) by @Abdennacer-Badaoui in [#49460] * docs: fix 'allows to' grammar in Vision Encoder Decoder docs (#48730) by @mrchatam in [#48730] * Fix SSH runner: add /opt/venv/bin to PATH for Python 3.11 images (#49759) by @ydshieh in [#49759] * Fix SmolVLM inputs_merger when image tokens are not a multiple of patch_size (#49725) by @albertvillanova in [#49725] * Ernie4.5-VL-MoE: shard the text and vision experts under TP and EP (#49462) by @IlyasMoutawwakil in [#49462] * Fix HunYuan-VL image assignment during batched generation (#49557) by @Arnav66692 in [#49557] ## Generation This release fixes a range of generation bugs: BLOOM crashes with static cache or compiled generate, `generate` dropping the type of dict-like inputs such as `ModelOutput`, and incorrect image assignment or placeholder handling in batched or beam-search generation for HunYuan-VL and Idefics2/3. It also fixes Qwen3-Omni audio generation mode handling, SAM mask-generation multi-zoom crops, empty frame s * fix: prevent empty frame sampling for short videos (#49908) by @BlazeSR10hawk in [#49908] * Fix Windows path separators breaking relative imports of Hub custom-generate modules (#48951) by @dltsum in [#48951] * Fix multi-zoom crops in the SAM mask-generation pipeline and related bugs (Fixes #35530) (#49689) by @stlukyanenko in [#49689] * update speculative decoding docs (#49697) by @merveenoyan in [#49697] * fix idefics3 generation issues (#49738) by @molbap in [#49738] * fix tests for generation (#49740) by @molbap in [#49740] * Fix inputs dict casting in `generate` (#49731) by @Cyrilvallez in [#49731] * [fix][Qwen3-Omni] Respect generation_mode in audio generation (#49505) by @Sunt-ing in [#49505] ## Parallelization This release extends parallelism support and fixes several related bugs. It adds a tensor-parallel plan for Nemotron and makes Ernie4.5-VL-MoE shard its text and vision experts under TP and EP. It also restores expert-parallel token-dispatch gradients on torch 2.7–2.10, fixes a Molmo2 model-parallel device mismatch, and corrects `base_model_prefix` in several model families (PP-OCR detectors * Add tensor parallel plan for Nemotron (#48780) by @Siddhant231xyz in [#48780] * fix model parallel bug for molmo2 model (#49816) by @kaixuanliu in [#49816] * Fix `base_model_prefix` in the PP-OCR detectors, CLIPSeg, TimesFM, CLIP and VideoPrism heads so base checkpoints load (#48871) by @blipbyte in [#48871] * Fix expert-parallel token dispatch gradients on torch 2.7 to 2.10 (#49710) by @digit50 in [#49710] * Skip Muse TP (#49717) by @remi-or in [#49717] ## Quantization Quantization now handles DeepSeek-V4.1's FP4 experts correctly: `FineGrainedFP8Config` gains an `expert_dtype` option ("fp8" by default, or "fp4") that the FP8 experts read instead of allocating them as FP8. TimesFM 2.5 no longer casts float inputs to an integer weight dtype when loaded with quantization such as bitsandbytes 4/8-bit. payload.name: Release: v5.21.0
payload.body: # Release v5.21.0 ## New Model additions ### MiniCPM-OCR MiniCPM-OCR is a document-understanding model from OpenBMB's MiniCPM-V family. It keeps the MiniCPM-V 4.6 architecture, which pairs a SigLIP vision encoder and a window-attention merger with a Qwen3.5 language model. It is specialized for reading text-dense images such as scanned pages, screenshots, receipts and tables. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/minicpm_ocr) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.18154) * Feat test (#49920) by @guarin in [#49920](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49920) ### Flint Flint is Recursive's mixture-of-experts language model. Compared to a standard SwiGLU MoE transformer such as Qwen3-MoE, it uses hybrid attention (sliding-window attention with rotary embeddings over the current token and the previous 512 tokens in most layers, and full attention without positional encoding in the remaining layers). It also has learned attention sinks, as in GPT-OSS, with per-head RMS-normalized queries and keys. Each sparse layer routes a token to 6 of 256 experts by sigmoid score and adds an ungated shared expert, and the first two layers are dense. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/flint) * Add Flint model support. (#49824) by @lovishmadaan in [#49824](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49824) ### UltraVBert UltraVBert extends ModernVBert by pairing the UltraBERT text encoder with a SigLIP vision encoder for visual document understanding and retrieval. Its image processor splits each page into 512-pixel tiles plus a global view. The connector merges each 4 x 4 block of vision patches into one token, so a tile becomes 64 image tokens, and RMS-normalizes them to the scale of UltraBERT's token embeddings. The `max_image_tiles` setting (27 by default) caps the number of tiles per page. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/ultravbert) * Add UltraVBERT (#49685) by @athrael-soju in [#49685](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49685) ### Gradium Phonon TTS Gradium Phonon TTS is Gradium's family of on-device text-to-speech models, trained with the Pocket TTS recipe. A causal transformer reads a voice prompt and the text, then emits one continuous 32-dimensional audio latent per step at 12.5 Hz through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when the utterance ends. The latents are decoded to 24 kHz audio by a Pocket TTS audio tokenizer. Unlike Pocket TTS, voice conditioning uses 512-dimensional latents from a separate, unreleased speaker codec, so voices come as precomputed latents and cannot be cloned from a recording. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/gradium_phonon_tts) * Add GradiumPhononTTS (#49791) by @eustlb in [#49791](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49791) ### Pocket TTS Pocket TTS is Kyutai's 100M-parameter text-to-speech model, built as a Continuous Audio Language Model that runs faster than real time on CPU. A causal transformer emits one continuous audio latent per frame (12.5 Hz) through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when to stop. A Mimi-based audio tokenizer encodes voice prompts and decodes the generated latents to 24 kHz audio. Two flow heads are released, Lagrangian self-distillation (default) and drifting, and voices can be cloned from a recording, passed as precomputed latents, or loaded from cached KV states. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (the Continuous Audio Language Models paper, arXiv 2509.06926). It is the only paper the documentation links, and it describes the architecture family Pocket TTS belongs to. The docs do not cite a separate Pocket TTS technical report.) | [Blog Post](NONE. The documentation links no official blog post. It points only to the original code repository at https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts.) * add PocketTTS (#49589) by @eustlb in [#49589](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49589) ### Pocket TTS Audio Tokenizer The Pocket TTS audio tokenizer is the codec used by Pocket TTS. It has Mimi's architecture (SEANet convolutions plus a small causal transformer on each side), but its residual vector quantizer is replaced by a continuous 32-dimensional bottleneck, the VAE-GAN from Continuous Audio Language Models. It converts 24 kHz audio into latents at 12.5 Hz and decodes them back to audio. It serves as the `audio_tokenizer` of `PocketTTSProcessor`, encoding voice prompts and decoding generated latents, and its encoder and decoder can also be loaded on their own. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts_audio_tokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (Continuous Audio Language Models, whose VAE-GAN this tokenizer uses; arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06926)) * add PocketTTSAudioTokenizer (#49588) by @eustlb in [#49588](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49588) ## Breaking changes Fixed Gemma4 processor imports (the Gemma4, Gemma4 unified and EmbeddingGemma2 processors) so `from transformers import *` no longer fails in environments that have `PIL` but not `torch`; no user action is needed. * :rotating_light: Fix gemma4 cross imports resulting in import failing without `torch` but with `PIL` (#49748) by @Sai-Suraj-27 Added an `"fp8"` backend to `QuantizedCache`, alongside `quanto` and `hqq`, that stores KV states in `torch.float8_e4m3fn` with a single scale per tensor; enable it with `cache_implementation="quantized"` and `cache_config={"backend": "fp8"}`. * 🚨Add an FP8 backend to `QuantizedCache` (#48677) by @jiqing-feng Tensor parallelism now has a dedicated embedding style, shards every model's input embeddings by default, and supports widths that aren't divisible by the TP size, so `ColwiseParallel` and `RowwiseParallel` now apply only to linear layers; custom TP plans that applied them to embeddings must switch to the new embedding style. * 🚨 TP: give embeddings their own style, shard input embeddings by default, and shard widths that don't divide by the TP size (#49570) by @IlyasMoutawwakil Every MoE TP and EP plan now shards its experts, so models no longer keep all experts on every rank, and a new `test_moe_parallel_plans_shard_experts` test enforces this; custom or downstream MoE parallel plans must add expert sharding to pass it and to avoid wasted memory. * 🚨 MoE: shard the experts in every TP/EP plan, and test for it (#49206) by @IlyasMoutawwakil ## Cache This release improves cache handling across the library. Flash Attention now works with static caches, BLOOM no longer crashes with static cache or compiled generate, chunked prefill supports cache continuation, and the Qwen4-Exp indexer's position history stays aligned with its cached keys. Linear-attention caches also gain new getters (`is_recording_past`, `get_recurrent_state`, conv-state access) that stop exposing cache internals and prepare for paged-c * [FA] Fix FA with static cache (#49998) by @Cyrilvallez in [#49998] * [docs] CB cache behavior (#49025) by @stevhliu in [#49025] * [CB] Reduce warmup time by not computing attention over full cache (#49853) by @remi-or in [#49853] * Fix Qwen4-Exp indexer position cache lifecycle (#49840) by @taking-lying-flat in [#49840] * [Cache] Linear attn cache: use new getters (#49375) by @remi-or in [#49375] * [Cache] Get conv states (#49309) by @remi-or in [#49309] * [Cache] Add get_recurrent_state (#49306) by @remi-or in [#49306] * [Cache] Add is_recording_past (#49305) by @remi-or in [#49305] * Fix BLOOM crash with static cache / compiled generate (#49481) by @kaixuanliu in [#49481] * Allow Cache continuation for chunked prefill (#49662) by @Cyrilvallez in [#49662] ## Vision Vision image processors now composite PNG transparency onto white instead of exposing black pixels, and `background_color` is preserved correctly across the DeepSeek-VL and Janus processors. Model fixes cover SmolVLM's `inputs_merger` when image tokens aren't a multiple of the patch size, HunYuan-VL image assignment during batched beam search, and Ernie4.5-VL-MoE expert sharding under TP/EP. It also fixes Qwen3-Omni audio generation mode handling, SAM mask-generation multi-zoom crops, empty frame s * fix: prevent empty frame sampling for short videos (#49908) by @BlazeSR10hawk in [#49908] * Fix Windows path separators breaking relative imports of Hub custom-generate modules (#48951) by @dltsum in [#48951] * Fix multi-zoom crops in the SAM mask-generation pipeline and related bugs (Fixes #35530) (#49689) by @stlukyanenko in [#49689] * update speculative decoding docs (#49697) by @merveenoyan in [#49697] * fix idefics3 generation issues (#49738) by @molbap in [#49738] * fix tests for generation (#49740) by @molbap in [#49740] * Fix inputs dict casting in `generate` (#49731) by @Cyrilvallez in [#49731] * [fix][Qwen3-Omni] Respect generation_mode in audio generation (#49505) by @Sunt-ing in [#49505] ## Parallelization This release extends parallelism support and fixes several related bugs. It adds a tensor-parallel plan for Nemotron and makes Ernie4.5-VL-MoE shard its text and vision experts under TP and EP. It also restores expert-parallel token-dispatch gradients on torch 2.7–2.10, fixes a Molmo2 model-parallel device mismatch, and corrects `base_model_prefix` in several model families (PP-OCR detectors * Add tensor parallel plan for Nemotron (#48780) by @Siddhant231xyz in [#48780] * fix model parallel bug for molmo2 model (#49816) by @kaixuanliu in [#49816] * Fix `base_model_prefix` in the PP-OCR detectors, CLIPSeg, TimesFM, CLIP and VideoPrism heads so base checkpoints load (#48871) by @blipbyte in [#48871] * Fix expert-parallel token dispatch gradients on torch 2.7 to 2.10 (#49710) by @digit50 in [#49710] * Skip Muse TP (#49717) by @remi-or in [#49717] ## Quantization Quantization now handles DeepSeek-V4.1's FP4 experts correctly: `FineGrainedFP8Config` gains an `expert_dtype` option ("fp8" by default, or "fp4") that the FP8 experts read instead of allocating them as FP8. summary:
## Liquid AI LFM3

[LFM3](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3) is Liquid AI's new family of small models built for local agents, tool calling, and structured output, on Liquid's new tri-hybrid architecture. The family includes:

- [lfm3](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3): a 1.7B text model with a 256K-token context window
- [lfm3-vl](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3-vl): adds image understanding
- [lfm3-audio](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3-audio): speech recognition, translation, and text-to-speech in 18 languages
- [lfm3-omni](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3-omni): text, images, and audio in one model

```sh
ollama run lfm3
```

## d1 decision models

Liquid AI's d1 models now come in a 2B size, built on LFM3. [d1](https://ollama.com/library/d1) makes decisions about text and images, and [d1-omni](https://ollama.com/library/d1-omni) adds audio.

```sh
ollama run d1:2b "I was charged twice for order 4417." --ask "Is this a billing issue?"
```

Note: lfm3 and d1 2b are supported on Apple hardware in this release.  Support for Linux/Windows coming soon.

## What's Changed
- Faster prompt processing on Apple silicon for Gemma 4, Flint and Laguna models
- Speculative decoding now supports DFlash2 draft models on MLX
- Gemma 4 keeps more detail in small images
- `ollama launch` now works with OpenCode v2
- Fixed tool-only assistant turns from Kimi CLI
- Updated MLX and llama.cpp

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.11...v0.40.12

summary: Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits.
